utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before I move on to the quote and the question, I would just like for the record that this is an excerpt from the book by Mr. Besim Ibisevic, "Srebrenica, 1987-1992."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please pay attention to what I'm going to read to you. The last sentence on page 175 reads: "Semso Jusic from the village of Poznanovic. A member of the Municipal Assembly for the village of Bozanovic told me that there had been shooting above their village the night before. The Bosniaks of Bozanovic spent the night in the open guarding their village. He also told me that the Serbs of the village of Fakovici had a store of weapons and ammunition stashed in an abandoned schoolhouse near the village of Ruljevici, in the municipality of Bratunac. The Serbs had received the arms from the JNA; Bosniaks had seen military lorries arriving in that village. I promised Semso I would personally go to Ruljevici and check whether there were any arms there. The Bosniaks had to know the truth." Mr. Redzic, let me ask you this: Do you know who Mr. Besim Ibisevic is?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to say a moment ago that he was the president of the municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether it is true that part of your life you spent working in the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked for 12 or 13 years in the Vlasenica bauxite mine. One part of this mine is in the territory of Srebrenica. And in view of the fact that many of our mines are scattered all over the area, the work itself was such and of that nature that it provided me with an insight into all the municipalities in the vicinity. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Ruljevici is? Is that a village? Is that a hamlet belonging to a village?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Ruljevici is a hamlet of the village called -- what is its name? Ruljevici is close to a hamlet near --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Redzic, is this a village somewhere on the border between Bratunac and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, between Bratunac and Srebrenica. Yes, it's a hamlet there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that at one of the meetings in April 1992, Mr. Ibisevic mentioned the events in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. You have assisted me, jogged my memory. It is this hamlet of Fakovici. Yes, they were discussing precisely these problems, both Mr. Ibran and Mr. Ibisevic, that weapons, equipment, and materiel were being transported across the Drina and concentrated in this area. In early April, the president of the Assembly, Mr. Ibisevic, told us that he had personally seen this. And as I will say later on in my testimony, I myself was able to see the things that were going on, and this was just a small part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's take it step by step. Please tell us: At these meetings, did they mention the villages near Drina, Fakovici and Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. They mentioned Fakovici and Bjelovac very often, saying that weapons, equipment, and materiel were being transported there across the Drina. They also mentioned Skelani on the banks of the Drina and they said what they had seen. They probably had no reason to lie about it. They said that there were already armoured vehicles there and heavy weapons, in Skelani that is, and the surrounding villages around Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At these meetings, was there any mention of Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Ratkovici sticks in my memory because they always said that helicopters were landing there, bringing in weapons, equipment, and materiel, and they linked this with General Zivanovic. I think that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- just to ensure that we have a very clear record. If the witness is referring to a day, are -- is he referring back to the meetings with Ibisevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ibisevic --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not testifying instead of him, but I -- that's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: There's -- I just want to make sure, Your Honour. There are lots of "they" in the record going on, and we just want to make sure that this is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any comments on what has been stated by Ms. Richardson, Mr. Redzic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will -- Your Honour, I'll deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will repeat my question to you. Did you hear about these events at the meetings with representatives of the municipalities where Mr. Ibisevic and Mustafic were also present?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the context I was referring to. We had those meetings and informed each other of the situation on the ground in these municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't sure whether your comment was in the transcript. Did you say that weapons were brought into the village of Ratkovici and that they linked it with General Zivanovic. Why did they link it with General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Because they said that he originated from the area, he was born there. And there was a reason because they often mentioned Ratkovici, together with General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, tell me whether I understood correctly that these meetings were held in late March and early April, 1992, these particular meetings that we are talking about now?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. In late March and early April, these meetings went on throughout 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Redzic. At these meetings in March and April 1992, was information brought forward by people who were representatives of the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was Mr. Nijaz Dubicic, the president of the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac, who gave us the most information about that. He gave us precise information about the Serbian villages around Bratunac. He said they were armed to the teeth, and he was frightened, as I was. None of us expected these things. What was most important in what he said about the events around Bratunac was that he kept mentioning the village of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. How often did this happen and what did he say with respect to Kravica, with respect to Kravica in 1991 until the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: In that period, according to his information, Kravica was already armed with automatic weapons and other kinds of weapons. And towards the end of 1991, there were open movements of armoured vehicles. You could see barrels in the surrounding hamlets around Kravica. And there was fear on the part of all Muslims. They dared not pass through Kravica even by daylight.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now ask that the video be played D696, and this is from Sarajevo television from September 1991, and it begins at 12.47. It's a very brief clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, please follow closely.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Nationality lost their lives. The situation is tense. According to Tanjug information, about 2500 Serbs, mainly women and children, have already moved to Ljubovija. Top people from the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina visited the spot today and held a press conference today in Sarajevo. In Kajici, Bratunac municipality, on the regional road, unknown persons set an ambush and fired from automatic weapons at four persons who were in a Lada vehicle with license plate number 280062. On this occasion, Nedzad Hodzic and Dzemo Jusic lost their lives and Mevludin Sinanovic and Zaim Salkanovic from the village of Repovci, Bratunac municipality, were wounded. Among the evidence we found bullet shells, fingerprints, and the forensic department is -- or, crime investigation department is already determining the factual situation. A large number of Muslims gathered and asked for weapons and requested that perpetrators be prosecuted in a way which is not in accordance with the legal system of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the same time, the Serb population whose large part had already moved to Ljubovija were disturbed. At this meeting we, Mr. Hebib and I, agreed with other representatives who were present there on what should be done officially as the Ministry of the Interior in order to reveal the perpetrators in a highly professional way with a maximum engagement of the ministry's forces. Secondly, we agreed to provide -- assisted their members of active and reserve forces, absolute peace and security, and, at this strike, this rally, Muslim representatives guaranteed, so to say, safety for all Serbs in the area of Bratunac."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, I will ask you the following: Are you familiar with this event in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Kajici is part of Kravica municipality?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vito Zepinic, who made these comments, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vito Zepinic is a Serb. He was assistant minister of the interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What you saw here, does it correspond to your information that two Muslims were killed and wounded, and could you please answer this part of the question first. Does this correspond with what you know?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully. This was so close to us and new words spread so quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, does this correspond with your information, what Mr. Zepinic said, that these people were killed from automatic weapons? Does this correspond to what you heard from Mr. Dubicic with respect to Kravica when he said that people were armed there with automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, because even if we hadn't believed Mr. Dubicic, Mr. Zepinic himself said what was going on and what there was in Kravica. His statement that a large number had moved out of Bratunac municipality. Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica, and Zvornik corresponds to his information but these were women and children. In other words, they had already prepared and pulled out people who were not fit for military service. And what remained behind was people who were able-bodied and ready at any moment to act against the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did this event upset the local Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Of course it did. It brought matters to a boiling point. The Muslim population didn't know where to go or what to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Up to now you have told us about information you received from members of the SDA, from the field, or from municipal officials in other areas. Did you also receive information in other ways, through other channels?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I mentioned, from the territory of my municipality, I received information from the Muslims there and also from the Serbs themselves. Serbs arrived in the municipality to complain. Because they came from remote villages, many of them were illiterate, as were many Muslims, and they would ask for the president; the secretariat would send them to me because Mr. Stanisic was probably not there at the time. And I would offer them a seat. I would offer them a cup of coffee. I would welcome them. And they told me openly that in the Serbian villages Serbs were distributing weapons, but that SDS members had priority and they were wondering when it would be their turn. I promised them that they, too, would be armed but then they shouldn't make a fuss about this. Later on I spoke to Mr. Stanic, the municipal president, and I told him I knew precisely what areas were settled and what time. He was surprised, not that they were distributing weapons; he was surprised that I had this information and he wondered how I got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what did the Muslims tell you? What happened at night, if anything, with regard to Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, this was already a prelude to the war. Muslims came from the area complaining, asking whether anyone could protect them because Serbs were firing from their houses, from automatic weapons. During the day, they set up roadblocks and barricades, and they issued open threats saying, "Turks, we will kill you all."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk about this with Mr. Milenko Stanic, the representative of the SDS, and if you did what did he tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: My conversation with Mr. Stanic was always open, at least as far as I was concerned. I wasn't preparing for war, and there were things he was unable to believe. We had some problems. For example, the village of Nedzeliste, because in the morning a group of Muslims --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, we'll come to that village. What I'm interested in now is what Mr. Stanic's position was, what his attitude was to the complaints of the Muslims? Did he try to do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. He was aware of it. He knew that the Serb areas were being armed. He knew they all had weapons. He was only surprised that I had certain information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I think it would be helpful to everyone if the witness could elaborate a little bit more on what Serb areas we're talking about, what Serb villages we're talking about. There's -- the record is going in rather vague and I think it would be helpful if he could specify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it will remain vague, Ms. Richardson. I can tell you I don't know how it fits in the case and how it's going to help the accused. But anyway, let's go ahead. Yes, please, Ms. Vidovic, if the witness can articulate which villages he's referring to one by one. This is what Ms. Richardson is interested in hearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be very happy to put this question, and I certainly will. However, the Defence case is such that it is very important to prove what this witness is talking about because he just said that there was firing from Serb houses, and I will go further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, what we are interested in is not whether this was firing in Serb houses two years before the events or a year before the events. Whether they were firing from Serb houses on the day when the various houses are alleged to have been destroyed, that's what we're interested upon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in any case, the Defence must prove that these people were armed in those villages, which would enable them to fire. So we will certainly come to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is, of course, relevant. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, let us go back to the question raised by the Prosecutor. Can you be specific with respect to the information you received and tell us what Serb villages it pertained to, what Serb villages were armed, and where was there firing from houses, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Nedzeliste, Hadzic, Sikosta [phoen] Rijeka, in this area north of Vlasenica. And from Milici towards Rupovo Brdo, from Derventa. There were Serbs as far as Zutica up there, and the same thing happened in all of these villages in Vlasenica municipality. Now we are talking of Nedzeliste, Sadici, and Sikosta Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about Podravanje?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Podravanje is concentrated up there. It is inhabited by Serbs and the tanks from Lukic Polje. Once or twice a day they went up there passing through the Muslim villages Dzile, Nurici, Bracani, Ilici, and so on. And they exerted in almost pressure, caused terror. I can't tell you what those people went through and they were cut off from neighbouring Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained the disposition of the military units which had arrived from Croatia. Can you explain to us whether in the course of 1990 and 1991 you had any knowledge other Serb military units on the territory of your municipality, if there were any?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: In the second half of 1991, there was a light brigade stationed in Milici on the playing field, that is on the stadium and next to it. And that was as early as the second half of 1991, at the beginning of the second half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know how many people were there who had military equipment?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: About 1.200 men. This was a light brigade and the soldiers from that brigade went to fight in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to Their Honours exactly how you learned of the existence of this brigade in Milici?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I had information from the people and I also passed through. But it was also on the media because this same brigade held a review in Milici and this was broadcast by Sarajevo Radio-television

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when this review took place?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I think it was in September and it was attended by the top leaders of SDS including officials from Serbia, such as Petar Gracanin. I think he was the minister of the interior at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The minister of the interior of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were told by people. What people and what did they tell you about this brigade? And was this a problem, in your view, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: This brigade was composed of people from Vlasenica municipality and these people had worked somewhere. As the president of the Executive Board and between -- I know that seven or eight of our employees went off to join that brigade, and this was illegal. And many managing directors from companies in Vlasenica municipality came to tell me that large numbers of able-bodied men of Serb ethnicity had been mobilised and were in Milici and that these people who had been mobilised and who were being paid by the JNA because they were printing money and they had lots of money, so those same men who were in the brigade and had been illegally mobilised were demanding salaries and they had to be paid their salaries, although they were not working. So under threat of arms, they had to give these people what they were not entitled to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned mobilisation. Was it legal mobilisation of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. It was illegal mobilisation and it was carried out by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did you learn about this? You mentioned the directors of certain companies. Can you be more specific? Which of the directors told you about this?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember Avdic Saban from the furniture factory who came to see me on the 10th of August and Mr. Ibran Nuhanovic, the director of the Birca forestry company. We talked about this topic and they said that those people were threatening them. I said "Well, you're intelligent men. Isn't it better to solve this rather than to cause a conflict, which is what the SDS and the army want?"

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about mobilisation also taking place in Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The pattern was the same. The scenario was the same. Everything I spoke about as happening in Vlasenica also happened in those other places. Only the place names differed, but the events were all the same and mobilisation was underway.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the official republican authorities, prohibit mobilisation and the departure of young men from Bosnia and Herzegovina to fight against Croatian Catholics in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina broadcast on television and informed us in dispatches and so on that the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not to be mobilised and sent to fight against Catholics in Croatia or against anyone else. And this was in line with their duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, try to do anything concrete to prevent illegal mobilisation and the sending of Muslim Bosniaks to go there and fight?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, this mobilisation was more legal than the one in Milici, Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik. This happened in late June 1991 when a light Vlasenica brigade with the 1.200 men was mobilised and the secretary for national defence was a Serb, Blagoje Colovic, and without my knowledge or the knowledge of the republican institutions he managed to mobilise this brigade and to dislocate [as interpreted] it to Han Pijesak, to the barracks there. In early July 1991, this same brigade was taken by truck to Zalozani and prepared to set out for Okucani in the Croatian war theatre. One morning in that period when the mobilisation was underway, I went there and I saw that the municipal building was surrounded by women, mothers, wives, sisters, daughters, and they were asking me to give them back their sons, their brothers, their husbands. I didn't even know where this unit was that had been mobilised. When I learned that they were in Okucani, I secured ten buses and a van and I collected those people. They got in and we went off to Zalozani so that the soldiers who had been tricked could be taken back to their towns, their villages, they factories, and their fields. I spoke directly to the general -- he wasn't a general at the time, he was a colonel, and he was the commander of the Zalozani area, Mr. Milosevic, his assistant was Asim Dzambasovic, and there was another assistant for security. Before the talks I formed a negotiating team with six others besides me, five Muslims and one Serb, and I have to mention that the Serbs did not accept mobilisation either. They didn't want their children to be sent to the war theatre and to kill the Croat-Catholic people or be killed themselves, because one gets killed in war. However, these officers refused to listen to what we said, and so I took it upon myself to tell the men to get on to the buses and to go to Vlasenica. I found buses from Banja Luka for the other people, and on the 4th of July I brought them back safe and sound to Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Redzic. Let me put another question to you. Did you then personally have problems because of this with the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The military Prosecutor Zivko Ostojic, as far as I can remember, filed a criminal report against me under Article 205, paragraphs 1 and 2, of the Criminal Code of the SFRY. I was accused of breaking up Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And were these proceedings ever completed?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No, because the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now put another question to you. Mr. Redzic, did the official authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina have the ability, in your view, to prevent the mobilisation of Serbs in that period from 1991 until the outbreak of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Realistically, no. Because they had already established their paramilitary institutions, they had their army. And the republican institutions, if the men in them were Serbs, they did not respect the decisions that they, themselves, adopted. The republican leadership was unable to take any measures and neither was the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now please show the witness document D99.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, would you please take a look at this document. This is a certificate, certifying that Milenko Jovanovic was mobilised on the 25th of March, 1992, to the Bjelovac TO and you see the signature of the company commander, Pero Petrovic. I will ask you to comment on this. Is it possible on the basis of the information you received and spoke about, that mobilisation was carried out in the Serbian villages in the Podrinje area as early as the 25th of March, 1992, and this refers to the Bjelovac TO but I'm asking you in general. Is it possible that mobilisation was carried out on the 25th of March, 1992, as it says in this document?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Mobilisation was carried out much earlier. This is a very late date. Mobilisation in all the areas, not just our subregion, but throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina was carried out much earlier. In this period where this person had been, maybe he hadn't responded to previous call-ups. But I'm surprised he was not mobilised earlier --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I was about to object simply to the phrasing of the -- the way question was posed, but I'll withdraw it at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, as you are talking about this mobilisation, did you tour this area and see for yourself that there was mobilised Serb forces on the ground? I'm referring to the time period from late March to early April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, before the witness answers, can we just have some clarity with respect to the area that was toured by the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's a proper observation, Madam Vidovic. So could you either rephrase the question or the witness is intelligent enough to follow-up from what has been stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will reformulate my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, in the second half of March and the first half of April, did you tour the Vlasenica municipality and did you see for yourself whether or not there were mobilised forces on the ground?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: It is true that I toured Vlasenica municipality, and I can list the villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, step by step. Did you make a tour at all?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I took every opportunity to have the president, Mr. Stanic, accompany me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You already said that Mr. Stanic was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, is it correct that on the 3rd of April, 1992, a meeting was held with the local leaders, including those of Srebrenica and Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I think it was our last meeting. After that, we didn't see each other again because very soon after that the fighting broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. The question that was last put to the witness by the Defence is clearly leading, and there have been a number of leading questions before. I have not objected, but I would only ask that the Defence refrain from putting leading questions to the witness, especially as we are getting into areas that are very relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That is also a correct observation. I think we have been quiet on this and we've cooperated because there were no objections forthcoming from your part. Now that, of course, there are objections, Ms. Vidovic will refrain from putting direct or leading questions. On the other hand, we would have appreciated not hearing from objections from your part if the leading questions are in reality harmless --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, we're dealing with an area and the time spent is marginally relevant at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, which is why I didn't object prior. But now we're getting into very relevant matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Ms. Vidovic, you've heard what I had to say. I mean, you know the distinction between a direct -- a leading question, which is not allowed when you are examining in chief. So I suggest you try to cooperate a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, is it true that you inspected the area with Mr. Stanic during this particular period of time.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Kindly, could you tell the Trial Chamber which villages you inspected together with Mr. Stanic?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: A large group of Muslims from Nedzeliste came and complained that the Serbs in the area, which was a mixed area inhabited by Muslim and Serbs, that the Serbs were shooting automatic weapons from their houses, they already wore S and B [as interpreted] uniforms, that they physically threatened them and so on and so forth. I called Mr. Stanic, told him what was going on in Nedzeliste and asked him to accompany me in the visits to this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber where Nedzeliste is?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The village of Nedzeliste is very close to Cerska and Skubric [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The two of us, the two presidents, took an official car and two policemen. And when we arrived in Nedzeliste not far from the primary school, we saw a unit of soldiers lined up in full military gear. They bore very peculiar insignia dating back from the Second World War, the ones the Chetnik used to wear. As a Muslim I was very surprised. I asked Mr. Stanic whether those were partisans. I wondered about the markings on the hats and I wondered whether those were 5-pointed stars. Stanic laughed and didn't comment. Later on the two of us --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Redzic. The men that you saw, did you know them? Did you know at least some of them?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I knew most of the people. They were all locals. It company commander I knew personally because his family was Prodanic and he worked in the Alpro factory in Vlasenica. He was a machinist there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you and Mr. Stanic do after that, if you did anything at all?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: After that I thought that we should call a number of prominent Serbs and Muslims and that we should call a meeting. I thought that by their reputation they could exert influence on the rest of the Serbs, that they should be drawing attention to the fact that there was no need for fire to be opened, for threats, because they had been neighbours for ages and that these things should not be happening. All those who were present there, the prominent Serbs who were there accepted that, promised that there would be no more problems, so that the Muslim population was calmed down by these words of the Serb representatives and their promises that this would no longer be happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that, Mr. Redzic, did you and Mr. Stanic visit any other Serbian villages?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Our route from then on was from Nedzeliste towards Sadici and then towards Lazarici hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were those Serbian villages as well?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, 100 per cent. Lazarici is 100 per cent Serbian hamlet which is connected with some other Serbian hamlets. Those were 100 per cent Serbian areas and hamlets.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether this is the same locality that you have just mentioned as a locality which bordered on a Muslim area?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the area which is some 6 kilometres away from Nedzeliste very close to Cerska, Sadici, and this hamlet Lazarici are close to Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, can you describe for the Trial Chamber what you saw there?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in Lazarici, we were stopped by two armed soldiers in olive-drab uniforms. They had automatic rifles. They stopped us. Their task was probably to ask for the ID of any passenger moving about. When Mr. Stanic and I got out of the car they probably recognised Stanic, and they did not ask for our IDs. We didn't have any problems with them. We were then encircled by a group of young boys aged between 12 and 15. Each and every one of them carried an automatic rifle on their shoulder or in their hands. I personally asked them, "Boys, where did you get the weapons from and what do you want the weapons for?" They answered that they were given the weapons by the army and that they needed them to defend themselves because the Turks from Cerska threatened to slaughter them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did the Serbian official, Stanic, react to that, the person who was with you?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: At that moment he did not say anything. He probably knew what was going on there. However, he opted -- the population was surprised by our arrival. There were no telephones, there were no mobile phones, nothing could be prepared for our arrival. Maybe he was even feeling sorry that he took me with him and I that saw, together with him, what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. During your inspection on that day, did you visit any other villages?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: As we were moving from Sadici to Vlasenica we came by another village. The area was mostly inhabited by the Serbs. We came by a village called Sikosta Rijeka. There is a primary school there and we found an identical situation there. Also there was a company lined up there, and what worried me most of all was the fact that the company was commanded by a person who was a member of the Municipal Assembly of Vlasenica, who at the time was over 65 years of age. From there, we set out to Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I put my next question to the witness I would like to learn from you where the next break is going to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next break should roughly happen now. However, since I have this appointment with the deputy registrar and also with the head of OLAD at 12.30, if we could go on for a few more minutes and then, say, have break within the next ten minutes or so, that would help me to keep appointments that I have because it will be difficult to fix appointments again with these two persons. So I think we would still be able to continue for the next ten minutes or so. And whenever you feel it's convenient for you to stop, just give me the signal, ask me, and we'll go -- we'll stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll certainly continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, did you, after having returned to the municipality of Vlasenica, did you submit a report on what you had seen?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. During that period of time in Vlasenica there was already a group of people representing the Serbs. This group consisted of six Serbs and also of six Muslims who represented the Muslims. They were in my office, and I informed this group about what I had seen in the area that I visited together with Mr. Stanic. I really didn't hide anything because Mr. Stanic was there with me. The members of this negotiating team were opposed, to my information, from the field. They didn't believe the word that I said; he called me a liar. I have to admit that Stanic was very correct at that moment and that he did say that the Serbian soldiers bore some very strange insignia on their hats.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stanic try to deny your words in any way?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. He was very correct. He kept quiet. And when he said something, he said that I was right, that my report was truthful, and that what I said about the Serbian soldiers and about their insignia was correct, that they bore the Chetnik insignia from the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he try to deny that the Serbs had already been mobilised on the ground, they wore uniforms?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No, I submitted a general report that there had been mobilisation, that the Serbs had weapons and uniforms, that they were well supplied. And the only thing that he said when his people objected and they said that I was exaggerating, he said, no, it's true what Redzic is saying and these people do bear some very strange insignia on their hats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just with respect to what was denied, again this is another form of leading the witness and I just would ask that more attention be paid to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is a legitimate question. I mean, unfortunately it's a repetition of -- it's inviting him to repeat what he stated earlier. Because if he had stated that Mr. Stanic bore him out and confirmed what he had been saying, I mean there was no need to ask him whether he tried to deny -- anyway, let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, what happened next with regard to this report of yours?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: After this report, the other members of Serb origin did not want to accept my report even after the words of their president, Mr. Stanic. They asked for a four-member-strong commission should be set up and that they should visit the same area that Mr. Stanic and I had visited before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did you look at that proposal on the setting up a new commission?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, it was nothing new under the sun. Whenever Serbs want to hide something, they use the method of setting up a new commission and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, from that moment on, what happened to you and other Muslims from the leadership of the Vlasenica municipality, from that moment on?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: From that moment on, many things happened. The war started on the 8th of April. This was the day when Zvornik was attacked and then Bratunac, Srebrenica, and Vlasenica, unperiled. At that moment from the end of March until the moment I left Vlasenica, a lot of Bosniaks had left the area. And during that period of time and after these meetings, as far as I can remember, we signed -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Very well then. At that moment in the area of Podrinje there was aggression, there was shelling, killing, the shelling of Zvornik, Skelani, Bratunac, and this moved on towards Srebrenica. The wave was moving on towards Srebrenica until the entire Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was occupied.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war started, did you have any information about the division of certain municipalities in the field, especially when it comes to --

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The principle was the same, the same thing that happened in Vlasenica happened elsewhere. In Srebrenica the Serbs wanted to see the municipality divided, in Zvornik as well, in Bratunac and Vlasenica. The principle was the same everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the division in Vlasenica, what happened there? What was your experience? What did the Serbs insist on in that area?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The document that I have says that the Serbs wanted the municipality of Vlasenica to be split into three parts, into the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica, the Muslim municipality of Vlasenica, and the municipality of Milici. There was no way out of that. There were threats coming from them. They said, "If you refuse to do that we will achieve it by blood, tanks, and expulsion." And as far as I remember on the 4th of April --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, let me ask you this: Before that, did you report the republican leadership about those events?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Of course I did. That was my duty after all. I could not have taken any risks upon myself. I reported directly to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic about the things that happened to us and what we were forced to do by the Serbs in the territory of Vlasenica. And all the -- the situation in all the other municipalities in the subregion, and in Bosnia and Herzegovina for that matter, was the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did Mr. Izetbegovic reply to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alija Izetbegovic said, and I quote: Mr. Redzic, do whatever and sign whatever in order to save as many people as possible. Stall as long as you can, stall the negotiations, try to prolong everything in order to enable as many people to leave the territory of Vlasenica because that -- those people were bare-handed. They didn't have any arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that did he mention the international community at all?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said to Mr. Izetbegovic, Izetbegovic, President, this is no joke; this is the end. The Serbs are armed to the tooth. There is no single house, there is no single child or an elderly person or anybody for that matter who doesn't have a weapon. At any given moment, the Muslims are threatened to be eradicated from the area. Mr. Izetbegovic says this should not happen; the international community will not allow this. And indeed, he was not aware of the situation on the ground. At many earlier meetings he said to us that we were too panicky, that the situation on the ground was not what we portrayed it to be. He trusted the international community too much and he was not in the least informed about the situation. Maybe he didn't want to know; I don't really want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I intend to use an exhibit after this. Maybe this would be the best moment for our next break and for me to wrap up this part of my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we'll have a break of 25 minutes starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Your Honour, I forgot to tender the transcript that you received along with the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, yeah, yeah, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it can be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's easy. That will become D696/T or dot 1, dot 1. All right. In the meantime just before you proceed -- before you proceed with you questions to the witness, I have had the meeting that I promised you I would seek a few minutes ago. But I suppose that you should -- the only thing that you ought to do is take up the matter with the head of OLAD, who's given me all the information that we required. I don't anticipate that there will be any problems; however, there is a protocol that is applied by OLAD to all lawyers that needs to be followed, and that is whether money is paid in advance or afterwards. We will also confirm in writing our expectations as to the estimated duration of this case, in other words for how long we expect you to be actively engaged until the end of your Defence case. And I have also explained in no unclear terms that we do expect you to be working these three weeks of August when we will be in recess -- not three weeks of August, but the summer recess. Part of it is in July, and most of it is in August. So that is the position. You will, of course, understand that we are not in a position to go beyond that and the matter is entirely in the hands of OLAD who has the discretion to decide on these things. But I don't think from what I have heard that you should have reasons for any particular reasons. That's it. So let's proceed. Let's not waste any more time. These 2 minutes you will not get back because I have --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've already got some help.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your support. Would the usher please show the witness document D604. For the record, this is a protocol of the agreement between the representatives of the Serbian and the Muslim people who were authorised by the representatives of the parties and council for inter-ethnic cooperation on the setting up of new municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, would you please look at this document and tell us whether you are familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course I am. This is a document that I signed together with the other five members representing the Muslim people. And on the other side there were six signatures from the ranks of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Chamber to whom you gave the original of this document?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I think the original was handed over to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in the course of other proceedings here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Redzic, you are familiar with this contents of this document. Can you briefly comment on it, please?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether one can comment on it briefly, because it shows that it was prepared very carefully over a long period of time. The other Muslims and I did not have anything to enter into it because we knew it would not create peace on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If you look only at these three municipalities, the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica and Milici municipality, you can see that this was done well and carefully prepared and that it was prepared by a group of experts, geographical survey experts, town-planning experts, and so on. On this document you can see that the lines separating of the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica and Milici municipality are very carefully drawn in great detail. And this was done by eminent experts who could not have prepared this within a brief space of time, so that this preparation had to have taken place over a much longer period of time in order to arrive at this division.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell Their Honours under what number on page 7 your signature is.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell Their Honours what happened to you after you signed this agreement.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I talked to Mr. Milenko Stanic, considering that he was the right person to tell me because I would have told him if something was being prepared for his people. And he personally told me that I should leave the territory of Vlasenica municipality and that there was nothing he could do to help me precisely because of the process and the army, the JNA, and the return of the mobilised soldiers. He was referring to the criminal report against me that I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How would you evaluate his attitudes towards you? Was it correct or not at that time?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to be fair and say that at that time he really did treat me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything else at the time that you feel is significant for further developments, something that you feel is important generally?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic told me that the area of Podrinje would be cleansed of Muslims completely and that what was left for the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina was the enclave of Tuzla and the enclave of Zenica. He told me not to go to Sarajevo because there would be rivers of blood flowing there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he mention the international community?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Bearing in mind that Muslims were leaving their farms and their hearths and their homes, I said to Mr. Stanic, you are persecuting us, expelling us bare-handed. The international community will help the people, the Muslims and the Catholics and maybe Serbs who might have been cleansed from other areas. And the international community will give us weapons and the Muslims will personally come perhaps with weapons to liberate what had been theirs for centuries. And he said to me, "Mr. Redzic, the international community is lying to you. They are telling you one thing and they are telling us something quite different." And to be sure, when I saw what happened afterwards, I often recalled Mr. Stanic and knew that it was really the way he said it would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened from that point onwards after the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Military operations started. The Serb forces attacked Zvornik on the 8th, before that Bijeljina, on the 4th at Bajram, on the 8th they attacked Zvornik, and then they continued along the river Drina against Bratunac and Srebrenica, and finally it was the turn of Vlasenica and many other municipalities throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you leave Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you submit any kind of report to the remaining authorities in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I informed people at the republican level as far as was possible. And on my arrival in Tuzla, I told them what had been going on and what might happen in the area around Tuzla also.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when you arrived there, did you continue your activities having to do with Podrinje and Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, when I arrived in Tuzla by way of Kladanj --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down a little bit because it's difficult for the interpreters to keep up with you and could you please make a brief pause between my question and your reply so that everything can be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I told you when I arrived in Tuzla via Kladanj, I started my work which I was duty-bound to do under the constitution and the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So what did you begin doing? What specifically did you do when you arrived in Tuzla? Who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: At that time, we applied to the Tuzla municipality and asked to be given some premises there because the municipality had premises at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And were you given premises?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, near the music school in a hut, a shed, which was owned by the Tuzla municipality, from Vlasenica municipality, Zvornik municipality, Srebrenica, Bratunac, all the officials who had --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, if I make a pause, I'm waiting for the interpretation. Could you please clarify: For what purpose were you given premises as well as the other people from the municipalities you have just mentioned? Could you please repeat that part?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: In connection with Vlasenica, we were given premises in order to continue our work concerning the large numbers of people who had been expelled from there, to provide minimum accommodation for them and what they needed to survive. As for the people from the other municipalities in the subregions, Zvornik, Srebrenica, and Bratunac, they were given premises in the same shed and they also formed their War Presidencies in exile.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: This was in late April or early May.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What year, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: First let me ask you this: What was your position in this dislocated War Presidency of Vlasenica in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I was the president of the War Presidency of the Vlasenica SO in exile.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From that point on, did you have any contacts with the people who formed similar bodies from Srebrenica - you call the War Presidencies - from Srebrenica and Bratunac who you said were in the same building?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that we were sharing the same building and that we had the same problems, it was quite logical for us to meet on a daily basis and exchange opinions, and what we learned from the ground from people who were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was your duty as the president of the dislocated War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Our task boiled down to receiving refugees, people who had been expelled, to providing accommodation for them and securing the minimum conditions for survival in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, did you talk to the people who arrived from these areas and can you tell Their Honours in what period people continued arriving in Tuzla from those areas?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: The period of the persecutions was in early April and it continued until the autumn. But one should not forget that many people continued to arrive. They were risking their lives. Many passed through the woods. Some were killed. Others managed to reach the free territory, so that people arrived in small groups through the woods and we interviewed them when they arrived, asking them what was going on in the areas they had come from.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And these people who arrived from Vlasenica, did they give you information about the overall situation in Vlasenica, or rather the area from which they fled regarding all aspects of their lives?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. These people were not just from the town of Vlasenica, it's a municipality with 507 square kilometres and they arrived from all over the municipality and they arrived in small groups and they gave us information about the situation in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now please show the witness D657.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document sent to the Ministry of Defence of Tuzla by Midhat Fejzic. Kindly look at this document it's name is: "Data, information." My question to you, first of all, is whether you're familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is this document about? Could you briefly comment on it? Did you ever see this document before you arrived here at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes because it was compiled by a man who was a member of the War Presidency, Midhat Fejzic, and he was in charge of the secretariat for national defence so that this is a report written by him. You can see that this was compiled in early 1994 and it incorporates all the previous reports of people arriving from the free territory when they were still able to arrive in buses or when the Serbs transported people by truck, and especially the people who walked through the woods to reach the free area, all these people provided information and each and every one of them was asked to describe the situation on the ground, whatever was important.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the last paragraph of this document where it says: "We do not have data on the material damage caused by the aggressor in the region of Vlasenica municipality, but we can claim with certainty on the basis of statements made by witnesses from this region that the damage is great and beyond calculation, particularly with respect to Vlasenica and its immediate surroundings, and the villages around it. There is not one village that has not been looted, torched, and destroyed. We do not have exact data on the total amount of the damage because the aggressor is still in the territory." So with respect to this, I wish to ask you the following: Does this document confirm that you, the War Presidency, received information in the way you have described?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only way we were able to get information, as I have just said. When people arrived from the area, they told us what had happened and in this last paragraph he says: "In Vlasenica and around Vlasenica all this territory was destroyed, burnt, looted, and places further away such as Cerska and Dzile, they were a kind of free enclave."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In your conversations with the people arriving, did you get information that among the refugees in Vlasenica, attempts were made to resist the Serbs? Did you have that kind of information at all or not?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Of course we did. The people who arrived from the area told us what had been destroyed, where; what had been burnt, where; where people had been killed. And we also received information that the free territory of our municipality, the area of Cerska, Dzile, and Jurici, Vrsinje near Suceska and near the Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you about armed groups, if they spoke about that at all?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the area towards the Srebrenica municipality. He had been the commander of the police station in Vlasenica, Mr. Fadil Turkovic and Mr. Becir Mekanic, in that area. As for Cerska, down there, there was Mr. Ferat Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about those groups fighting the Serbs there trying to get something done?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did have information because people who were respected in the area had the role of protecting the refugees and the Muslim people in the area of Dzile and below Dzile, bordering with Suceska as well as Cerska itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The refugees who arrived, did they describe the situation on the ground? Did they tell you how these groups were organised, whether or not they were organised?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: As for organisation, these were self-organised local people led by the two men I have named on the territory of Vlasenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the information being given to the witness, there's reference to the refugees giving information. I would ask that we have some reference to names, if the witness knows, so that we create a picture that doesn't entirely seem like hearsay and what they said exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've been receiving hearsay for the past eight months, nine months plus, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I think your observation is very valid and if the witness can identify by name any particular persons from these refugees that were passing on this information to him, then please go ahead, please do. I very much doubt where we are going -- where we are going to get. You said, Mr. Redzic, that there were refugees passing this information on to you. Do you recall any one in particular amongst these refugees by name that the Prosecution can then identify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this was a large number of people. Of course, it would be unnatural if I couldn't remember any of them, but there were 5 or 6.000 people who had left that territory in various ways, on foot, by bus, by truck. One such man was Mumin Ademovic [phoen] who lives in the Netherlands today. Later on he was employed in Vlasenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, I will ask more questions in this direction because we also wish to know who provided this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when one of the commanders you mentioned, himself, arrived in Tuzla, a leader of the one of the local groups?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Towards the end of October 1992, Mr. Becir Mekanic arrived on the free territory of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at that time have a detailed talk with him about how he had organised his group, what his relations were with other fighters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because again, this is the kind of leading questions that you shouldn't be putting, especially on this -- in this area of evidence. Did you meet this Mr. Mekanic? Did you have a meeting with him when he arrived in the free territory of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, and we continued coordinating our activities until he was killed. I met him and we coordinated our activities until he was killed in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. When you met him the first time, what did you discuss? What was discussed between you or amongst you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our discussion was mainly about general information, about refugees, about humanitarian organisations, about the military resistance, and I'm referring to the self-organised spontaneous resistance of the local people. He often told me that there was chaos, that humanitarian conditions were chaotic, that there was an enormous amount of refugees who had been in the woods a long time, and he himself was a local man. He was influential in the area, and he tried to organise resistance and save the refugees, the Muslim refugees in the area. Of course he had huge problems. There was no army there, there was no chain of command, and he went to Cerska sometime in September I think. And he told me that there was no cooperation, that cooperation was very poor, that individuals were denying what others were doing, that they were engaged in a kind of power struggle. And this weakened the organised resistance that the Muslims were offering in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, did he mention any names of commanders with whom he did or did not cooperate?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. He most often mentioned Zulfo, who was from the area of Suceska, and his arrogance. This made Mr. Mekanic leave the area and go toward Cerska. And then in late October, as I said, he came to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to understand from what he said whether between Mr. Mekanic and others on the ground there was any kind of superior-subordinate relationship?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: On the contrary. There was conflicts and there was no coordination. It was self-organised people trying to save what they could while individuals were trying to gain the upper hand over each other and there was no kind of subordination. There was even animosity between or among those individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this what Mr. Mekanic told you?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke to Mr. Mekanic. We had many conversations between 1992 and 1995 about everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now please show the witness document P123. For the record, this is a document issued by the District Staff of Tuzla of 28th of September, 1992. It's a report on the staffs and units and the institutions that had been set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, could you please take a look at page 01827485, and towards the bottom of the page it says "Municipal Defence Staff of Vlasenica." Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me first ask you this: Can you look at what it says under items 1 through 10, and can you tell us whether you had any information about anything that is described herein about the existence of the units which are listed here in the area that you've mentioned a while ago in the area of Srebrenica and Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see here the Defence Staff of the municipality of Vlasenica. A reference is made to the TO Vlasenica, TO Cerska and TO Dzile. These are the areas that I have spoken about and this document was probably in the possession of my secretary for defence, Midhat Fejzic. And if you're asking me how this happened --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Redzic. Let me draw attention to this. This -- the date is 29 August 1992. Let me ask you this: People who arrived from the field including Mekanic, did they tell you about these units that existed as units that existed in Vlasenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said that the area where Mr. Mekanic was, where Mr. Fadil Turkovic was, those were the so-called free territories of Vlasenica. The other part is Cerska and there were indeed the staffs of Territorial Defence there. I believe that this information was also brought by many people who arrived through the woods and when they arrived to the corps they provided the security of the 2nd Corps of the BiH army with this information. And I believe that they drew up the document based on that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, could you go two pages forward and can you please look at the page 018271484. Could you please look at the part entitled "the Municipal Staff of the Defence of Srebrenica." And let me ask you this: What was your information from the people who arrived, and especially from Mr. Mekanic, about the relationship between the fighters from Vlasenica and the fighters from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: As for the relationship, I have already said that the relationship was almost non-existent. Srebrenica was too far from this area and so were the Cerska and Srebrenica units. This is 15 kilometres from the territory that was under the control of the Serbian army, and as for the parts which were under the control of Fadil Turkovic and Becir Mekanic, there was also no cooperation between them and the Srebrenica TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, did Mr. Mekanic tell you that?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Of course. Becir Mekanic repeated that, and it was this lack of cooperation that made him to go towards Cerska and further on towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else. Did you know Ferid Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ferid Hodzic was the commander of the TO of the Municipal Staff of Vlasenica before the war. When the war broke out, he left for Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this document that you have mentioned, reference is made to the Cerska detachment. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time during the war when Ferid himself appeared in Tuzla, Ferid Hodzic, that is?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: When Cerska fell in February, Ferid Hodzic arrived with a large group of soldiers, to put it that way, from Cerska. And he broke through to the free territory of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And after that, did you talk to Mr. Ferid Hodzic and how did he describe the situation that prevailed in the territory of Srebrenica and Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Of course that we talked. We had constant conversations. He personally told me that in Cerska, in the territory of Cerska, there was a disaster. The army was not armed, certain groups or local individuals, commanders, failed to be disciplined. They fought for power. They did not very much care about the organisation of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, could you tell us when did Ferid Hodzic arrive in Tuzla? You said when Cerska fell. Can you put it in a time context?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: It was in February 2003.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What year, once again? You said 2003?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 1993. I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You also told us that you knew Ferid Hodzic very well. Did you talk to him specifically about the events that happened in Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Of course I did. We had a lot to talk about. Those things were a priority and we discussed them at great length.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to him about the organisation of the units in that area? And how did he describe that organisation to you?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We discussed that and he said that there were some individuals in the area who were arrogant, who were not responsible, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did he mention any attempts to consolidate the resistance in the enclaves? Did he mention anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. He mentioned the organisation of the subregion or the setting up of the subregion. I believe that this happened sometime in November 1992, according to him. There was a meeting in Konjevic Polje. The intention was to consolidate the political and military structures in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what did he tell you about that? Was the intention ever carried through? What did he tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: No, it never happened. He said that this never took off the ground. There was a meeting, there were some proposals, but he said that this never functioned, this never took off the ground, and he really did not want to accept the proposals that were put forth at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, can you tell the Trial Chamber what Mr. Hodzic told you? Why was he -- what was he proposed for in the subregion?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: He said that Mr. Hamed Salihovic was put forth on behalf of the civilian authorities as the president of the subregion, that Mr. Naser Oric was put forth as the commander of the subregion, and that he, himself, was proposed as the chief in the subregion. And indeed he said that he never accepted to be a chief under Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, based on what he told you, did you gain the impression that he was ever under the command of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: According to what he said, I would never say that he was under that command. The question is whether he could ever be during that short period of the establishment of that subregion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what he told you -- he told you, if anything, about his reasons for not accepting the position of the chief of the subregion?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: According to him, there was a general disaster in the area. The Serb forces during that period of time, when they met in November, had already started a major offensive. They shelled everything that could be destroyed in the area, and the physical separation of the units from Srebrenica from the units in Cerska and Konjevic Polje was also a factor. So this just could not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the record we would like to explain. I asked the witness about the reasons why he didn't accept to be the Chief of Staff, and all this time on the record we have the word "chief," which may lead to a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you understand me when I asked you about his position of the chief, that it was position of the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... convenient for you. And we will continue tomorrow morning in this courtroom. I thank you. In the meantime, Mr. Redzic, just one small piece of information that I need to give you. You haven't finished with your testimony and therefore that -- Mr. Redzic, I need to inform you that since you have not finished your testimony as yet and that you will continue tomorrow, you are not to communicate with anyone or let anyone communicate with you and discuss in any manner the contents of the -- of your testimony and the events that you are testifying about. So I have your word for that. We'll reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of July, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
